newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Sweden bids for U.N. Security Council seat.
newsitem.headline: Sweden bids for U.N. Security Council seat.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson on Wednesday urged the U.N. to elect his country to the Security Council, saying it would take independent positions upholding international law.

"If elected to the council, Sweden would continue to pursue openness and transparency. The links between the council and the U.N. membership must be strengthened," he said in a speech to the General Assembly.
"Sweden would take independent positions, upholding the principles of international law. The primacy of international and humanitarian law is a pillar of our foreign policy," he added.
The General Assembly is expected to hold elections in October to choose five countries to replace those whose two-year terms on the 15-member Security Council expire on December 31.
Sweden, Australia and Portugal are vying for two seats reserved for members of the U.N. regional group called West European and Others, due to be vacated by Germany and Italy.
Persson said Sweden's candidacy was launched with the full support of the other Nordic countries -- Denmark, Finland, Iceland and Norway.

He said council members had a particular responsibility for international peace and security and it was essential that small and medium-sized countries should serve on the council, whose five permanent, veto-bearing members are the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France.
Sweden has served on the council twice before, in 1957-58 and in 1975-76.

Persson said Sweden would contribute to a "more efficient U.N. role in the 'new generation of peacekeeping,' including a better coordination between civilian and military aspects of such operations." It would also work for clearer mandates for U.N. operations, he said.
